entries.speaker: Albert Einstein
entries.quote: I cannot substantiate my attitude to physics in such a manner that you would find it in any way rational. I see of course that the statistical interpretation (the necessity of which in the frame of the existing formalism has been first clearly recognized by yourself) has a considerable content of truth. Yet I cannot seriously believe it because the theory is inconsistent with the principle that physics has to represent a reality in space and time without phantom actions over distances.... I am absolutely convinced that one will eventually arrive at a theory in which the objects connected by laws are not probabilities, but conceived facts, as one took for granted only a short time ago. However, I cannot provide logical arguments for my conviction, but can only call on my little finger as a witness, which cannot claim any authority to be respected outside my own skin.
entries.work: Letter to Max Born, reproduced within Max Born's own text (Waynflete Lectures, published as "Natural Philosophy of Cause and Chance"), Part X "Metaphysical Conclusions", as hosted on informationphilosopher.com's Max Born page
entries.locus: informationphilosopher.com/solutions/scientists/born/, quoted by Born directly following the sentence: "The second letter, which arrived just when I was writing these pages (dated 3 December 1947), contains this passage:"
entries.note: This is BORN'S OWN TRANSLATION (not Doyle's paraphrase) — Born quotes the German original in full immediately before the English rendering on the same page: "Meine physikalische Haltung kann ich Dir nicht so begründen... ohne spukhafte Fernwirkungen.... Davon bin ich fest überzeugt... keine Autorität, die ausserhalb meiner Haut irgendwelchen Respekt einflössen kann." The English above is the parenthetical translation printed immediately after the German on that page, ending with an ellipsis ("....") exactly as printed — this ellipsis is Born's own, not an editorial omission by me. Page is hosted by Bob Doyle's Information Philosopher site but the block-quoted passage itself is Born's, reproducing his 'Natural Philosophy of Cause and Chance' lectures (the source volume that also contains this letter appears in the published Born-Einstein Letters collection). entries.speaker: Albert Einstein
entries.quote: I consider it quite possible that physics cannot be based on the field concept, i.e:, on continuous structures. In that case, nothing remains of my entire castle in the air, gravitation theory included, [and of] the rest of modern physics.
entries.work: Bob Doyle, "My God, He Plays Dice!" — Chapter 38, "Einstein's Field Theory" (section "Castle In The Air")
entries.locus: Chapter 38, p.316-317 (section "Castle In The Air"); Doyle's footnote 2 on this quotation cites "Pais, 1982, p.467" (Abraham Pais, "Subtle is the Lord")
entries.note: This is DOYLE'S RENDERING as printed in his book text, introduced with: "In 1954 Einstein wrote his friend Michele Besso to express his lost hopes for a continuous field theory like that of electromagnetism or gravitation, ‘...quote...’" Doyle's own citation attributes the translation to Pais 1982 p.467, not to a primary Einstein-archive translation of his own — i.e. Doyle is reproducing Pais's rendering of the Besso letter, not independently translating it. Retrieved by fetching the full PDF text via r.jina.ai (direct WebFetch summarization of this same PDF returned only a truncated preface excerpt, chapters 1-4, and separately claimed the later chapters were not in its context window).

entries.speaker: Albert Einstein
entries.quote: I must confess that I was not able to find a way to explain the atomistic character of nature. My opinion is that if the objective description through the field as an elementary concept is not possible, then one has to find a possibility to avoid the continuum (together with space and time) altogether. But I have not the slightest idea what kind of elemen-tary concepts could be used in such a theory.
entries.work: Bob Doyle, "My God, He Plays Dice!" — Chapter 38, "Einstein's Field Theory" (section "Castle In The Air")
entries.locus: Chapter 38, p.317; Doyle's footnote 3 cites "Stachel, 1986, p.380"; Doyle's own inline citation reads "(Einstein to David Bohm, 28 October 1954)"
entries.note: DOYLE'S RENDERING, introduced with: "In the same year, he wrote to David Bohm, ..." Citation attributes translation to John Stachel 1986 p.380, not an independent Doyle/Born translation. The word break "elemen-tary" is a hyphenation artifact of the source PDF's line-wrap, reproduced here verbatim as extracted. For cross-check only (NOT the retrieved primary text used above, wording differs slightly): a WebFetch of Wikiquote's "De Broglie–Bohm theory" page returned the same passage with "if an objective description" (vs. Doyle's "if the objective description") and "than one has to find" (vs. Doyle's "then one has to find") — flagging this as a known variant wording across secondary sources; the Doyle/informationphilosopher.com text above is what was actually requested and retrieved.

entries.speaker: Richard Feynman
entries.quote: What do we mean by “understanding” something? We can imagine that this complicated array of moving things which constitutes “the world” is something like a great chess game being played by the gods, and we are observers of the game. We do not know what the rules of the game are; all we are allowed to do is to _watch_ the playing. Of course, if we watch long enough, we may eventually catch on to a few of the rules. _The rules of the game_ are what we mean by _fundamental physics_. Even if we knew every rule, however, we might not be able to understand why a particular move is made in the game, merely because it is too complicated and our minds are limited. If you play chess you must know that it is easy to learn all the rules, and yet it is often very hard to select the best move or to understand why a player moves as he does. So it is in nature, only much more so; but we may be able at least to find all the rules. Actually, we do not have all the rules now. (Every once in a while something like castling is going on that we still do not understand.) Aside from not knowing all of the rules, what we really can explain in terms of those rules is very limited, because almost all situations are so enormously complicated that we cannot follow the plays of the game using the rules, much less tell what is going to happen next. We must, therefore, limit ourselves to the more basic question of the rules of the game. If we know the rules, we consider that we “understand” the world.
entries.work: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I
entries.locus: Chapter 2, §2-1 "Physics before 1920" (paragraph 5 of the section, per the site's own paragraph numbering)
entries.note: Underscored words (_watch_, _The rules of the game_, _fundamental physics_) mark italics in the source's own HTML/markdown rendering, preserved here as printed by the reader tool. feynmanlectures.caltech.edu returned a Cloudflare block page to direct curl requests and gave inconsistent, partial/paraphrased output over several WebFetch attempts (the tool repeatedly cited an unexplained '125-character quote limit' not present in my request and refused full reproduction); this full paragraph was instead retrieved via the r.jina.ai text-extraction mirror of the same URL, and the opening and closing sentences were independently cross-verified as exact character-for-character matches against two separate successful WebFetch passes (one direct, one via goodreads.com's quotation of the same opening sentences). entries.speaker: Richard Feynman
entries.quote: In this chapter we shall tackle immediately the basic element of the mysterious behavior in its most strange form. We choose to examine a phenomenon which is impossible, _absolutely_ impossible, to explain in any classical way, and which has in it the heart of quantum mechanics. In reality, it contains the _only_ mystery. We cannot make the mystery go away by “explaining” how it works. We will just _tell_ you how it works. In telling you how it works we will have told you about the basic peculiarities of all quantum mechanics.
entries.work: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume III
entries.locus: Chapter 1, §1-1 "Atomic mechanics" (opening paragraph of the chapter)
entries.note: Underscored words (_absolutely_, _only_, _tell_) mark italics as rendered by the r.jina.ai text extraction of the page. Text independently cross-verified as an exact match against a separate direct WebFetch pass on the same URL, which returned the identical wording. Date is the volume’s publication year (Vol. I 1963, Vol. III 1965); the lectures were delivered 1961–63. The source page carries no date of its own.

entries.speaker: Richard Feynman
entries.quote: It is all quite mysterious. And the more you look at it the more mysterious it seems. Many ideas have been concocted to try to explain the curve for P 12 in terms of individual electrons going around in complicated ways through the holes. None of them has succeeded. None of them can get the right curve for P 12 in terms of P 1 and P 2.
entries.work: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume III
entries.note: "P 12", "P 1", "P 2" are how the site's subscripted symbols (P₁₂, P₁, P₂, rendered as MathJax/LaTeX $P_{12}$ etc. in the original) came through the plain-text extraction — the subscript digits are printed with a preceding space rather than as true subscripts; this is an extraction artifact, not a content difference. entries.speaker: Richard Feynman (as recounted by Feynman, quoting his father)
entries.quote:
The next Monday, when the fathers were all back at work, we kids were playing in a field. One kid says to me, “See that bird? What kind of bird is that?”
I said, “I haven't the slightest idea what kind of a bird it is.”
He says, “It's a brown-throated thrush. Your father doesn't teach you anything!”
But it was the opposite. He had already taught me: “See that bird?” he says. “It's a Spencer's warbler.” (I knew he didn't know the real name.) “Well, in Italian, it's a Chutto Lapittida. In Portuguese, it's a Bom da Peida. In Chinese, it's a Chung-long-tah, and in Japanese, it's a Katano Tekeda. You can know the name of that bird in all the languages of the world, but when you're finished, you'll know absolutely nothing whatever about the bird. You'll only know about humans in different places, and what they call the bird. So let's look at the bird and see what it's doing — that's what counts.” (I learned very early the difference between knowing the name of something and knowing something.)
entries.work: What Do You Care What Other People Think? — Part 1, "A Curious Character": "The Making of a Scientist" (1988)
entries.locus: Part 1, "The Making of a Scientist", page marker {3}-{4} in this online transcription
entries.note: This is the BOOK version, distinct in wording from the 1966 NSTA speech version below — note the invented mock place-names here are "Spencer's warbler / Chutto Lapittida / Bom da Peida / Chung-long-tah / Katano Tekeda", where the NSTA version instead used real-sounding "brown-throated thrush / halsenflugel (German) / chung ling (Chinese)" with no Spencer's-warbler misdirection and no Italian/Portuguese/Japanese entries. Italics in the original (e.g. book/place names) are not distinguishable in this plain-text scrape; none appeared present in this passage regardless. entries.speaker: Richard Feynman (as recounted by Feynman, quoting his father)
entries.quote:
So we went alone for our walk in the woods. But mothers were very powerful in those day's as they are now, and they convinced the other fathers that they had to take their own sons out for walks in the woods. So all fathers took all sons out for walks in the woods one Sunday afternoon. The next day, Monday, we were playing in the fields and this boy said to me, "See that bird standing on the stump there? What's the name of it?"
I said, "I haven't got the slightest idea."
He said, 'It's a brown-throated thrush. Your father doesn't teach you much about science."
I smiled to myself, because my father had already taught me that [the name] doesn't tell me anything about the bird. He taught me "See that bird? It's a brown-throated thrush, but in Germany it's called a halsenflugel, and in Chinese they call it a chung ling and even if you know all those names for it, you still know nothing about the bird--you only know something about people; what they call that bird. Now that thrush sings, and teaches its young to fly, and flies so many miles away during the summer across the country, and nobody knows how it finds its way," and so forth. There is a difference between the name of the thing and what goes on.
entries.work: "What Is Science?" — address to the National Science Teachers Association, New York City, 1966 (published in The Physics Teacher, Vol. 7, No. 6, 1969, pp.313-320)
entries.locus: p.4 of this PDF transcription (page-break marker "4" appears mid-passage in the source scan, between "the Catskill" and "Mountains for vacations" a few lines above this excerpt)
entries.note: This is the 1966 NSTA SPEECH version, distinct in wording from the 1988 book version above. Note the mixed straight/curly quotation marks and the stray apostrophe in "He said, 'It's a brown-throated thrush..." and "those day's" — reproduced exactly as they appear in the PDF's extracted text (likely OCR/typesetting artifacts of this particular scanned transcription rather than of Feynman's original delivery).
